accuracy.evidence: Matches the interoception and body-map research: Nummenmaa et al. (2014) found anger felt in the hands and upper body and anxiety in the chest and stomach, which is where flag_soma.js places clenched fists, racing heart and butterflies. The 'body alarm' is a child-level account of the fight-or-flight stress response, and the slow-breathing step reflects evidence that slow paced breathing lowers arousal. It does not claim one clue always means one feeling.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the mix-ups 7 to 9 year olds really make: treating butterflies as hunger (step 2 prediction, challenge tag need), thinking a racing heart always means scared (step 3 slide versus barking dog, tag one), believing strong body feelings mean you are ill (tag ill) and that feelings stay only in your head (tag none). The adult text names these as common mistakes.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is about where feelings show in the body: dragging four clue cards onto a body outline, decoding clues into feelings, comparing one heartbeat across two scenes, turning a body-alarm dial up and breathing it down, and a head-to-toes body scan of Sam before a school play. None of this fits the existing feelings-naming, triggers or calming labs by swapping labels; it passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step adds one part of the idea: clues live in body places, a clue can be decoded, context decides between excited and scared, the alarm readies the body and slow breaths calm it, and a scan in order ends with naming the feeling. The learner places and tests first; the done message only confirms what the canvas showed.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Butterflies in your tummy. Does that mean you are hungry?', 'Your heart is racing. Does it always mean you are scared?' and 'Can slow, deep breaths turn the alarm down?' (many children say you just have to wait). Each is tested on the canvas, and the reveal says what the learner predicted and why the answer differs.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions such as Zara's racing heart at a fun camp and Tom's stiff shoulders. Every wrong option carries a tag with its own message, e.g. 'A racing heart can mean scared or excited. Look at what is happening to tell which.' and 'That mixes a feeling clue with a body need.' Choice order rotates each turn.

readability.evidence: Family audience: kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete words (tummy, fists, heart, shoulders) and pass the FK 5.0 target; adult paragraphs pass 10.0 and cover scope, the alarm idea, named mistakes and a tour of the lab. Every canvas clue pairs an emoji with a word so a pre-reader can follow with a grown-up.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate passed. Kid sentences are rules or examples (butterflies before a test, fists when cross). Hints point at the scene or the body part, e.g. look at what is happening, rather than general praise. No repeated template lines between steps.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 (390 px) screenshots before and after Show me on every step: the body outline and four clue cards fit with big tap targets, the two heart scenes stack full-width, the alarm dial and its Alarm up and Slow breath buttons are reachable with one thumb, and the body-scan list does not clip. Desktop text was enlarged after an earlier check found it too small.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (clue buttons, Alarm up, Slow breath, scan part buttons, feeling choices). The canvas aria-label updates with each message, feedback is in words not colour alone, and walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA with no violations in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
